newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania welcomes World Bank loan, needs more funds.
newsitem.headline: Romania welcomes World Bank loan, needs more funds.

text.p: Romanian Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea welcomed on Thursday an $80 million World Bank loan to restructure industry but analysts warned that more funds were needed to sustain the long-term drive to reform.
"The credit is good. Actually we fulfilled all criteria agreed with the World Bank to get it so we had no emotions in this respect," Ciorbea told Reuters.
On Tuesday, the World Bank gave Romania an $80 million loan of an existing $280 million Financial and Enterprise Structural Adjustment Loan (FESAL).

The loan was released by the World Bank after Ciorbea's government brought in a law on portfolio investment and announced steps to restructure the regies autonomes, which form the core of the industry and include the state-run utilities.
Ciorbea's centrist cabinet, which ousted ex-communists in last year's general election, pledged quick, firm action.
A Western analyst in Bucharest said the release of the $80 million loan was a signal sent by the Bank to foreign investors that reforms in Romania were on the right track.
"The government should do its best to match words with deeds if it wants to maintain a credible profile among foreign investors," the analyst said.

About $100 million of the $280 million FESAL credit had been disbursed last year when the World Bank suspended credits to Romania, saying the leftist government of the time had failed to meet reform commitments.

A final $100 million tranche of the credit is subject to government's meeting a series of new targets including the privatisation of 850 companies, 50 of them big enterprises, plus two state banks and closure of loss-making companies.
Last month, the World Bank approved $550 million in credit package to Romania to help restructure the farming sector, upgrade infrastructure and cushion the effects of reforms.
The International Monetary Fund also gave Romania a fresh stand-by facility of $430 million in April after endorsing the new government's reform programme.
A local analyst said more funds were needed to "bridge" the programmes agreed with the two international lenders.

"One should have in mind that there is always a risk for Romania to create gaps between the short-term stabilisation achieved with IMF money and the long-term targets agreed with the World Bank," he said. "Such gaps could compromise reforms."
Boosting private small and medium-sized companies could help Romania create a "sound segment" able to sustain growth and soften the effects of shock-therapy reforms, he said.
"I also think a credit of around $100 million, to be used only in cases of emergency to prevent sudden movements in the economy, could be helpful," he said whithout elaborating.

"The gap theory is logical," the Western analyst said. "However, I think foreign investments coming from the private sector are the key to Romania's future growth rather than credits. This could be an answer on how to fill those gaps."
So far, foreign direct investments in Romania stand at at mere $2.45 billion since the 1989 overthrow of communism.
